source_refs.note: Book p. 38-39: 3.3.2 Absolute Value Quadratic Inequalities, Example 6 with its two number lines (stops before Exercise 3.1); callouts marked Teaching note / Key points / Common mistake and the Book correction boxes are ours.

blocks.text: Absolute value quadratic inequalities are inequalities that involve a quadratic expression within absolute value bars. They are generally of the following form:

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Turn the absolute value into ordinary inequalities with the rules from 3.3 (here \(d > 0\)):
\(|E| < d\) becomes \(-d < E < d\): two inequalities joined by "and"; the answer is the common part (intersection) of their solutions.
\(|E| > d\) becomes \(E < -d\) or \(E > d\): the answer is everything in either solution (union).
Then solve each quadratic inequality by the critical-number method:
1. Bring everything to one side and compare with 0.
2. Solve the equation \(= 0\) to get the critical numbers.
3. Mark them on a number line: they split it into regions.
4. Test one point from each region; keep the regions where the inequality is true.
5. Use open ends for \(<\), \(>\) and closed ends for \(\le\), \(\ge\).

blocks.title: Example 6
steps:
Given: \(|x^{2} - 6x - 4| < 3\).
To find: all real \(x\) satisfying the inequality, as a set of intervals.
Method: \(|E| < 3\) means \(-3 < E < 3\). This gives two quadratic inequalities, (i) and (ii), that must both hold. Solve each by finding its critical numbers (roots) and testing one point in each region of the number line; then take the common part (intersection).

Step 1: Remove the absolute value
\[|x^{2} - 6x - 4| < 3\]
\[-3 < x^{2} - 6x - 4 < 3\]
Why: a number whose distance from 0 is less than 3 lies between \(-3\) and \(3\).

Step 2: Split into two inequalities
The book writes \(-3 < x^{2} - 6x - 4\) or \(x^{2} - 6x - 4 < 3\). Both parts must hold at the same time, so the joining word is "and":
\[-3 < x^{2} - 6x - 4\]
\[\text{and}\quad x^{2} - 6x - 4 < 3\]
Why: \(-3 < E < 3\) is short for "\(-3 < E\) and \(E < 3\)".

Step 3: Bring everything to one side
\[x^{2} - 6x - 4 + 3 > 0\]
\[x^{2} - 6x - 1 > 0 \quad \text{...(i)}\]
\[x^{2} - 6x - 4 - 3 < 0\]
\[x^{2} - 6x - 7 < 0 \quad \text{...(ii)}\]
Why: comparing a quadratic with 0 lets us use its roots as boundary points.

Step 4: Critical numbers of (i): solve \(x^{2} - 6x - 1 = 0\)
\[x = \dfrac{-(-6) \pm \sqrt{(-6)^{2} - 4(1)(-1)}}{2(1)}\]
\[x = \dfrac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 + 4}}{2} = \dfrac{6 \pm \sqrt{40}}{2}\]
Why: it does not factorize with integers, so we use the quadratic formula with \(a = 1\), \(b = -6\), \(c = -1\).

Step 5: Simplify the roots
\[x = \dfrac{6 \pm 2\sqrt{10}}{2} = 3 \pm \sqrt{10}\]
\[x = 3 - \sqrt{10},\quad 3 + \sqrt{10}\]
\[x \approx -0.16,\quad 6.16\]
Why: \(\sqrt{40} = \sqrt{4 \times 10} = 2\sqrt{10}\), and \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.162\). Hence the critical numbers divide the number line into three regions (Figure (i) below).

Step 6: Test one point in each region of (i)
Test \(x = -1\): \((-1)^{2} - 6(-1) - 1 > 0 \Rightarrow 6 > 0\) (True)
Test \(x = 0\): \((0)^{2} - 6(0) - 1 > 0 \Rightarrow -1 > 0\) (False)
Test \(x = 7\): \((7)^{2} - 6(7) - 1 > 0 \Rightarrow 6 > 0\) (True)
Solution set of (i) is \((-\infty, -0.16) \cup (6.16, \infty)\).
Why: a quadratic can change sign only at its roots, so one test point decides the whole region.

Step 7: Critical numbers of (ii): solve \(x^{2} - 6x - 7 = 0\)
\[x^{2} + x - 7x - 7 = 0\]
\[x(x + 1) - 7(x + 1) = 0\]
\[(x + 1)(x - 7) = 0\]
\[x = -1,\quad x = 7\]
Why: two numbers with product \(-7\) and sum \(-6\) are \(1\) and \(-7\). These critical numbers divide the number line into three regions (Figure (ii) below).

Step 8: Test one point in each region of (ii)
\(x = -2\): \((-2)^{2} - 6(-2) - 7 < 0 \Rightarrow 9 < 0\) (False)
\(x = 0\): \((0)^{2} - 6(0) - 7 < 0 \Rightarrow -7 < 0\) (True)
\(x = 10\): \((10)^{2} - 6(10) - 7 < 0 \Rightarrow 33 < 0\) (False)
Solution set of (ii) is \((-1, 7)\).
Why: same reasoning as Step 6.

Step 9: Take the common part
Hence the solution set of the given absolute value quadratic inequality is, as the book prints it,
\((-\infty, -0.16) \cup (6.16, \infty)\} \cap \{(-1, 7) = (-1, -0.16) \cup (6.16, 7)\)
Written with balanced brackets:
\[\{(-\infty, -0.16) \cup (6.16, \infty)\}\]
\[\cap\ (-1, 7)\]
\[= (-1, -0.16) \cup (6.16, 7)\]
Why: both (i) and (ii) must hold, so we keep only the numbers in both sets. On the number line: from \(-1\) to \(-0.16\) and from \(6.16\) to \(7\).

Check:
\(x = -0.5\) (inside): \(|0.25 + 3 - 4| = 0.75 < 3\). True.
\(x = 6.5\) (inside): \(|42.25 - 39 - 4| = 0.75 < 3\). True.
\(x = 3\) (in (ii) but not in (i)): \(|9 - 18 - 4| = 13\), not \(< 3\). Correctly excluded.
\(x = -1\) (end point): \(|1 + 6 - 4| = 3\), not \(< 3\). Correctly excluded (open interval).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book splits \(-3 < x^{2} - 6x - 4 < 3\) into "\(-3 < x^{2} - 6x - 4\) or \(x^{2} - 6x - 4 < 3\)". It must be "and": a double inequality means both parts hold together. With "or" the answer would be the union of (i) and (ii), which is every real number, and that is wrong (for example \(x = 3\) gives \(|-13| = 13\), not less than 3). The book itself correctly takes the intersection at the end.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The final line is printed with unbalanced brackets: "\((-\infty, -0.16) \cup (6.16, \infty)\} \cap \{(-1, 7) = \ldots\)". It should read \(\{(-\infty, -0.16) \cup (6.16, \infty)\} \cap (-1, 7) = (-1, -0.16) \cup (6.16, 7)\). The result itself is correct.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: \(-0.16\) and \(6.16\) are rounded values of \(3 - \sqrt{10} = -0.1623\ldots\) and \(3 + \sqrt{10} = 6.1623\ldots\). The exact answer is \((-1,\ 3 - \sqrt{10}) \cup (3 + \sqrt{10},\ 7)\); in an exam, give the exact form and the decimals together.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(|E| < d \Leftrightarrow -d < E < d\) ("and", intersection).
2. \(|E| > d \Leftrightarrow E < -d\) or \(E > d\) ("or", union).
3. Solve each quadratic inequality with critical numbers and test points.
4. Open circles and round brackets for strict inequalities \(<\), \(>\).
5. Check with a point inside and a point outside the final answer.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Using "or" (union) for \(|E| < d\): it is "and" (intersection).
2. Testing only one region: test every region, because the sign of a quadratic can change at each critical number.
3. Including the end points in a strict inequality.
4. Mixing up the signs when moving terms: \(-3 < E\) becomes \(E + 3 > 0\), not \(E - 3 > 0\).
